cards.claim: IFNSO reduces computational cost of orthogonalization by replacing iterative Newton-Schulz blocks with a single unified operation
cards.conditions: General orthogonalization in optimizers like Muon; applicable to neural network optimization
cards.effect: Reduces matrix multiplications along the long dimension from N to 1
cards.evidence: Proposed as primary contribution and core novelty of the method
cards.quote: a single-pass operator with learnable parameters designed to replace traditional iterative blocks, reducing the number of matrix multiplications along the long dimension from N to 1

cards.claim: IFNSO achieves lower FLOPs than standard Newton-Schulz iterations while maintaining competitive orthogonalization error
cards.conditions: Matrix orthogonalization; tested on matrices of sizes 1024×1024, 2048×2048, 4096×4096
cards.effect: FLOPs reduced to O(km) vs O(knm) for other methods; computational burden grows slower as matrix size increases
cards.evidence: Table 1 comparative experiments on matrix operations
cards.quote: Our method demonstrates competitive efficiency by reducing the number of computationally expensive operations from to , where is more costly than because . This advantage stems from its lower cost of floating-point computations, achieved by reducing the amount of computation along the -axis. Specifically, as increases, the computational burden of our method grows more slowly compared to other methods.

cards.claim: IFNSO integrated into Muon optimizer achieves best loss and competitive accuracy on MNIST in short training runs
cards.conditions: MNIST dataset, simple neural network, Muon optimizer, batch size 32, max 10 epochs, cross-entropy loss
cards.effect: Loss of 4.25 (best among methods tested) and accuracy of 98.87%
cards.evidence: Table 2 comparative experiments on optimization performance; Figure 7 convergence curves
cards.quote: the network optimized using our strategy yields the best performance. Correspondingly, Figure 7 demonstrates that the model trained with our NS iteration algorithm achieves the fastest convergence.

cards.claim: IFNSO achieves fastest convergence speed compared to other Newton-Schulz iteration variants with Muon optimizer
cards.conditions: MNIST dataset, 10 epoch training runs, Muon optimizer, batch size 32
cards.effect: Training loss decreases faster over iterations, reaching convergence sooner
cards.evidence: Figure 7 training loss curves showing IFNSO (labeled 'Our') descending below other methods throughout training
cards.quote: the model trained with our NS iteration algorithm achieves the fastest convergence

cards.claim: IFNSO uses learnable coefficients and exponential term selection to maintain orthogonalization quality while reducing computations
cards.conditions: Polynomial-based orthogonalization with depth n; optimization via Adam with learning rate scheduling
cards.effect: Balances computational cost against approximation accuracy; satisfactory performance at n=5
cards.evidence: Section 2.3 coefficient optimization and Section 3.3 ablation study
cards.quote: Increasing consistently improves the expressive capacity of the polynomial, leading to lower approximation error on the target interval. However, beyond a certain depth, the performance gain saturates, while the computational burden gradually increases. Therefore, we set as our default for the matrix.
